title: elastic-respite-windows-and-tiered-burst-contracts-prd-draft
body:
Purpose
This doc proposes a new Dedicated product feature: Elastic Respite Windows (ERW) + Tiered Burst Contracts. The goal is to give tenants predictable, low-cost reserved capacity while offering controlled, reversible relaxation of strict isolation during short bursts. ERW is a safety-first mechanism to enable occasional over-commit with bounded impact to co-tenants and clear operational semantics for preemption, billing, and observability.

Context & Motivation
Today Dedicated customers buy reserved pools to guarantee throughput and latency. They also expect strong isolation — but many customers have spiky workloads and are willing to accept short, managed risk of degraded latency or limited preemption if it lowers cost and reduces wasted idle GPUs. Current approaches are either: 1) strictly isolated (wasteful at low utilization), or 2) opportunistic burst into shared capacity (unpredictable). ERW aims to bridge that gap with a controlled, productized contract.

Key principles
- Bounded impact: any relaxation must have a hard, observable bound on latency and error rate impact to other tenants.
- Reversible & auditable: changes to isolation are explicit, time-limited, and logged for billing/audit.
- Predictable economics: customers know the burst allowances and pricing ahead of time.
- Safety-first defaults: platform should default to never violate SLA without explicit tenant opt-in and ops guardrails.

User personas
- Platform Engineer (tenant): wants predictable budget and to avoid paying for large idle tail.
- Product Platform (customer): needs burst behavior during planned events (campaigns) and clear failure modes.
- Site Reliability / Operator: needs observability and emergency runbook to revoke respite windows quickly.

Success metrics (initial)
- Reduce percent of idle GPU hours on committed pools by 15% among pilot tenants.
- <1% incidence of cross-tenant SLO breach attributable to ERW in first 6 months.
- Pilot tenants report >80% satisfaction with cost/availability tradeoff in survey.

Scope (what this PRD covers)
- Definition of Elastic Respite Windows and the Tiered Burst Contract model.
- API and console UI surfaces for configuring contracts and respite windows.
- Runtime admission and preemption semantics, plus telemetry & alerts.
- Billing model and invoicing events tied to respite usage.
- Operational runbook and revert controls.

Out of scope
- New hardware-level isolation primitives (e.g., MIG partitions).
- Full multi-cloud marketplace pricing — price formula will be regionalized in follow-up.
- Deep research into kernel-level scheduler changes.

High-level product model
1) Tiered Burst Contract
- Commitment tiers: Bronze / Silver / Gold. Each tier defines a capped burst budget (vGPU-hours) per billing window, priority class for preemption, and price multiplier for tokens consumed while in burst.
- Example: Bronze = 10% additional capacity for 30 minutes/day at 1.8x unit price; Silver = 25% for 2 hours/day at 1.5x price; Gold = 40% for 6 hours/day at 1.2x price.

2) Elastic Respite Window (ERW)
- An ERW is a time-bounded window where tenant isolation constraints are relaxed to allow the tenant to exceed their reserved pool up to their tier cap.
- ERW must be scheduled (planned) or can be requested on-demand with a short approval/verification step if quota remains.
- Respite windows are enforced by the capacity broker and runtime admission: when enabled, tenant requests are allowed to borrow a limited number of slots from a soft pool of opportunistic capacity.

API & Console surfaces
- Contract management endpoints (create/modify/cancel contract) exposing: tier, committed_capacity, burst_cap, billing_multiplier, preemption_priority, retention_period.
- ERW scheduling endpoints: schedule_respite(start_ts, end_ts, expected_peak_rps, reason, emergency_flag).
- UI: contract summary, upcoming scheduled respites, recent respite usage, and per-route impacts (latency distribution during respites).
- Alerts: automatic note to tenant when ERW triggers any hard preemption or when cross-tenant latency delta exceeds threshold.

Admission & preemption semantics
- Soft borrow: During ERW, tenant can exceed reserved pool but the platform will obey the following: 1) prefer idle capacity in the tenant's own pool; 2) borrow marked opportunistic capacity across dedicated pools to the extent allowed by burst_cap; 3) if platform load increases, opportunistic allocations are revoked in inverse order of tier priority (Bronze first).
- Preemption levels:
  - Soft preemption: CPU/GPU work is throttled (reduced slot shares) but KV caches preserved; used as first-level mitigation.
  - Hard preemption: active allocations are terminated and requests receive a 503/429 depending on policy; used when SLO risk for higher-priority tenant exceeds guardrail.
- Safety guardrails:
  - Global SLO monitor: if platform-level latency for a hardware pool exceeds configured deviation, all ERWs touching that pool are automatically suspended.
  - Tenant-level cap: each ERW request cannot exceed the per-tenant minute-rate defined by burst_cap_rate.
Observability & telemetry
- Per-tenant ERW timeline: start/end, borrowed_slots, preemption_events, average tail latency delta, token consumption at burst pricing.
- Dashboards: pool-level heatmaps showing ERW borrow levels and co-tenant SLO anomalies.
- Tracing hooks: link from preemption events to request traces and rollback events in the console.

Billing model
- Dual-meter: baseline usage billed as before; any token/compute during ERW above reserved allocation billed at burst multiplier.
- Burst credit balance: tenants with unused burst budget can sell back credits at a discount if they opt-in to a marketplace (future). For MVP, unused credits simply expire at billing window end.
- Invoicing: ERW lines appear in billing detail with start/end and tokens consumed under burst multiplier.

API examples (illustrative)
- POST /contracts {"tier":"silver","reserved_gpus":4,"burst_cap_minutes":120,"burst_cap_percent":25}
- POST /respite/schedule {"contract_id":22,"start":"2026-03-01T18:00:00Z","end":"2026-03-01T20:00:00Z","expected_rps":1200}

Acceptance criteria (MVP)
- Tenant can create contract and schedule ERW via API and Console.
- Runtime admits bursts up to configured cap for pilot tenants and records borrow metrics.
- Automatic suspension of ERWs when pool-level SLO deviation > 10%.
- Billing records show burst-metered consumption in the invoice preview for the current window.
- Operator can revoke all ERWs for a pool with a single action and that action is logged.

Rollout plan
- Q1 internal alpha with 3 pilot customers (opt-in) on two dedicated pools. Instrument aggressively for telem and feedback.
- Q2 expand to 10 customers, expose Bronze/Silver tiers; refine pricing.
- Q3 public beta with console UI and 1-click opt-in; measure platform-level impact and iterate on guardrails.

Operational runbook (summary)
- Detection: alert from pool heatmap → runbook: query active ERWs in pool → if > threshold, escalate.
- Emergency revoke: operator console provides "suspend ERWs in pool" button. Post-incident: run blame & invoice adjustment flow.
- Postmortem data: all revoked ERWs must be annotated with reason and follow-up action.

Risks & mitigations
- Risk: cross-tenant SLO breaches. Mitigation: strict default guardrails, immediate suspend on threshold, run simulation load tests.
- Risk: customer confusion about pricing. Mitigation: clear console billing preview and FAQ/one-pager during purchase flow.
- Risk: operator overhead. Mitigation: automated suspension and revert tooling; initial pilot with dedicated SRE owning incident runbooks.

Open questions
- What is the right default burst multiplier per region? Finance input needed.
- Should there be an on-chain/event-driven audit trail for eviction decisions? Ops/Legal to weigh in.
- Do we allow automatic scheduled recurring ERWs (weekly/monthly)? Might complicate capacity forecasting.

Appendix: Example tenancy scenario
Tenant A purchases 8 reserved GPUs (Gold). Typical utilization 50% but needs a 6-hour marketing spike once monthly. They choose Gold tier which grants 40% additional capacity for up to 6 hours. They schedule an ERW for the planned window — the runtime borrows opportunistic capacity, their latency stays within 1.1x baseline for 95th percentile, they are billed at 1.2x for tokens above 8 GPUs. If the platform experiences a sudden high-priority tenant surge, opportunistic allocations are revoked preferentially from Bronze→Silver→Gold, and Tenant A may see throttling or terminated requests; all events are surfaced.

Next steps
- Engineering spike: capacity broker prototype to simulate ERW borrow and preemption ordering (2 sprints).
- Finance: propose initial price multipliers and model revenue impact (1 sprint).
- UX: console wireframes for contract purchase and ERW scheduling (1 sprint).

Notes to reviewers
- Look for unclear safety semantics or missing operator controls.
- Suggest telemetry items we might be missing (per-epoch tail-latency, KV cache hit-rate changes during ERW, etc.).
